hook.text: Your head is aging faster than your feet. Right now. Measured, in a lab. And that is the smallest example of something much darker.

b-nist.text: In twenty ten, physicists at NIST raised one atomic clock just thirty-three centimeters above another. The higher clock ticked faster. Over a seventy-nine year lifetime, your head ages about ninety billionths of a second more than your feet.

h-jila.text: And thirty-three centimeters is nothing. Twelve years later, physicists shrank that experiment down to a distance you can barely see.

b-jila.text: Inside a single cloud of strontium atoms, a clock resolved time running faster across just one millimeter of height. The top of the cloud... aged faster than the bottom.

h-gps.text: This isn't a lab curiosity. Your phone corrects for broken time... every single day. Let me show you.

b-gps1.text: Twenty thousand kilometers up, a GPS satellite's speed slows its clock by seven microseconds a day. But weaker gravity speeds it up by forty-five. Gravity wins — by thirty-eight microseconds, every day.

b-gps2.text: So engineers detune every GPS clock before launch. It is built deliberately wrong on Earth... so that it becomes right in orbit. Uncorrected, the error would equal about ten kilometers of ranging drift, every single day.

h-core.text: Now aim that same physics straight down. Because the deeper you go into the Earth... the slower your clock runs.

b-core.text: Over four and a half billion years, gravitational time dilation has made the center of the Earth about two and a half years younger than the ground you are standing on.

b-feynman.text: Richard Feynman famously guessed the difference was a day or two. He was wrong by a factor of a thousand — and nobody checked the math for over fifty years.

h-iss.text: So what happens to an actual human being who leaves the planet? We ran that experiment. With identical twins.

b-iss.text: On the space station, gravity is still nearly full strength — so speed dominates. Orbiting at twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour slows an astronaut's clock far more than the altitude speeds it up.

b-kelly.text: After three hundred forty days in orbit, astronaut Scott Kelly returned about five milliseconds younger than his identical twin brother Mark. He time-traveled. Into the future.

h-moon.text: And this is about to become a real engineering crisis. Because we are going back to the Moon... and the Moon runs on different time.

b-moon.text: Lunar clocks gain fifty-six microseconds every single day. That is why NASA is building Coordinated Lunar Time right now — an official clock for another world.

b-mars.text: Mars is worse. A Martian clock runs four hundred seventy-seven microseconds a day faster than Earth's. And the rate itself wobbles, as Mars swings closer to and farther from the Sun.

h-sun.text: Everything so far has been microseconds. Now let's step into a real gravity well... and watch time visibly bend.

b-sun.text: On the surface of the Sun, clocks fall behind Earth's by about sixty-six seconds every year. Stand there for a lifetime... and you would return more than an hour into the future.

h-wd.text: Then we pointed Hubble at the corpse of a dead star... and watched time genuinely crawl. Sirius B packs the mass of our Sun into a ball the size of Earth.

b-wd.text: Hubble measured its light, stretched by gravity — clocks there lose about two point four hours every year.

b-ns.text: On the surface of a neutron star, general relativity predicts time itself runs roughly twenty-five to thirty percent slower. Live one year there... and about sixteen months pass everywhere else.

h-s2.text: But the deepest clock experiment in history didn't use a clock at all. It used an entire star... falling toward a supermassive black hole, at a distance of just 120 astronomical units.

b-s2.text: In twenty eighteen, the star S2 swung past Sagittarius A star at nearly three percent of the speed of light. Its light stretched exactly as Einstein predicted — a century after he wrote it down.

h-miller.text: So could Interstellar really happen? One hour on that planet... seven years on Earth. Here's what the physics says.

b-miller.text: Kip Thorne did the math. It works — but only around a black hole spinning within one part in one hundred trillion of the maximum the universe allows.

b-quote.text: Thorne's own verdict: possible in principle... implausible in nature. The universe allows it. It just probably never built one.

h-twist.text: And here's the part that should genuinely unsettle you. You would never feel any of this. Your clock always ticks normally... it's everyone else's that drifts.

b-now.text: GPS satellites. The Moon. Mars. The Sun. Every star in the sky. No two clocks in the universe agree. There is no master clock. Now... only exists where you are standing.

cta.text: Time isn't one river — it's billions of them, all flowing at different speeds. Subscribe to mindwired... yours is running out.
